There are technical inconsistencies in the formulation. The policy-gradient theorem is written without an explicit action expectation; the KL constraint is stated as KL(new || old) but the estimator/objective appears to use samples from the old policy and log pi_old/pi_new, corresponding more closely to KL(old || new) up to constants; the entropy-augmented reward is indexed inconsistently in the pseudocode; and the HL-Gauss loss is written without the usual negative sign. These may be presentation errors, but they undermine confidence in the derivation.

The method is described as fully on-policy, yet it performs multiple epochs over stale trajectories, optimizes the actor on newly sampled actions under a critic trained only on behavior-policy actions, and relies on KL control rather than a principled correction. The paper should be more precise about what is actually on-policy and what approximation is being made.

The empirical comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Several baselines are imported from prior work or run with fewer seeds, different implementations, different horizons, and unclear tuning budgets. The claimed superiority over PPO, SAC, and FastTD3 is therefore hard to attribute cleanly to the proposed pathwise estimator.

The ablations do not isolate the main claim strongly enough. The score-based/pathwise comparison is confounded by learned-Q quality, variance reduction choices, entropy/KL tuning, and architecture. There is little direct analysis of critic accuracy, surrogate bias, action-distribution shift, or when the pathwise gradient becomes misleading.

Claims of hyperparameter robustness are insufficiently supported. The paper says one hyperparameter set works broadly, but gamma and value-support bounds are adapted per environment, and there are no convincing sweeps over KL target, entropy target, critic capacity, update epochs, batch size, or auxiliary-loss weight.

The wall-clock and memory claims are weaker than stated. Wall-clock results compare only JAX REPPO to PPO and omit key off-policy baselines because of framework issues, while memory is discussed mostly through buffer size rather than measured end-to-end memory footprint.

Presentation and reproducibility need work. The manuscript contains typos, missing cross-references, a truncated code-availability sentence, small/hard-to-read aggregate figures, and incomplete implementation details that are deferred to the codebase. For a complex RL algorithm, this is not enough to make the results easy to reproduce or audit.

The paper overclaims significance relative to the evidence. The results are promising, but the evidence does not yet justify broad claims about unlocking pathwise gradients for on-policy RL or being robustly superior across sample efficiency, wall-clock time, memory footprint, and hyperparameter robustness.
